questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Describe the layered structure of the Earth paying particular attention to:

(i) Variation in composition;

(ii) Physical states.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Earth (mean radius about 6 371 km) is made of concentric layers, known from the behaviour of **seismic waves** (changes of speed and reflection at boundaries, the S-wave shadow zone behind the core), from meteorites, from xenoliths and from the density of the planet. A labelled section of the Earth is credited.

**(i) Variation in composition (the chemical layers).**

| Layer | Depth | Composition | Density (g per cubic centimetre) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Continental crust** | average about 35 km (20 to 70 km) | Upper part **felsic (granitic)**, rich in silicon and aluminium ("sial"); lower part more mafic (intermediate to basic) | about 2.7 |
| **Oceanic crust** | about 5 to 10 km | **Basaltic** (basalt, dolerite and gabbro), rich in silicon and magnesium ("sima") | about 2.9 to 3.0 |
| **Mantle** | from the Moho to about 2 900 km | **Ultramafic** silicate rock (peridotite): olivine and pyroxene, rich in Mg and Fe; lower mantle in dense high-pressure silicates | about 3.3 to 5.5 |
| **Core** | 2 900 km to 6 371 km | An **alloy of iron and nickel** with a little of a lighter element (sulphur, oxygen or silicon) | about 10 to 13 |

The **Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)** separates the crust from the mantle (seismic velocity of P waves rises from about 6.5 to about 8 km per second), and the **Gutenberg discontinuity** at about 2 900 km separates the mantle from the core.

**(ii) Physical states (the mechanical layers).**
- **Lithosphere** (about 100 km thick on average): the **rigid, brittle outer shell** made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, broken into the tectonic plates.
- **Asthenosphere** (from about 100 km to about 250 or 350 km): a **weak, plastic, partly molten (about 1 per cent) layer** of the upper mantle that flows slowly, where seismic waves are slowed (the low velocity zone); the plates move over it.
- **Mesosphere (lower mantle)** (to 2 900 km): **solid but hot and able to flow very slowly** (convection currents), because the high pressure makes it more rigid with depth. A transition zone at about 410 to 660 km has changes of mineral structure.
- **Outer core** (2 900 to about 5 150 km): **liquid** (S waves do not pass through it, and P waves are slowed and refracted, causing the P-wave shadow zone); the convection of this liquid iron produces the Earth's magnetic field.
- **Inner core** (about 5 150 km to the centre): **solid**, because of the very high pressure (more than 3 million atmospheres), in spite of a temperature of about 5 000 to 6 000 degrees Celsius.

The temperature increases with depth (the geothermal gradient is about 25 to 30 degrees Celsius per km in the crust), and the pressure also increases.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Discuss the genetic classification of folds.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **genetic classification of folds** classes them by **the way (mechanism) in which they were formed**, which depends on the direction and the nature of the stress and on the behaviour of the rock layers. The main genetic types are:

1. **Buckle folds (compressional folds, active folds).** Formed when a **competent layer is shortened by compression parallel to the layering**, so that it buckles. Two mechanisms: **flexural slip** (the layers slip over one another like the pages of a book, so that the thickness of each layer stays constant and **parallel (concentric) folds** result), and **flexural flow** (the layers flow, with thickening at the hinge). The wavelength depends on the thickness and competence of the layer. They are the **commonest folds of fold mountain belts**, such as the Alps and the Appalachians.
2. **Bending (forced or drape) folds.** The layers are **bent by a vertical force acting at right angles to the layering**, often by the movement of a fault in the basement: the cover rocks are draped over the rising fault block (**monoclines**), or over an intrusion (laccolith) or a rising **salt dome (diapiric folds)**. The beds above are arched without lateral shortening.
3. **Shear folds (passive or similar folds, slip folds).** The layers are **passive markers**, which are sheared along numerous closely spaced **parallel slip planes (shear or cleavage planes)** at an angle to the layering, so that the thickness along the limbs changes but the shape of the folds is the same in each layer (**similar folds**, thicker at the hinge). They are found in highly deformed metamorphic rocks.
4. **Flow folds.** Formed in **very ductile or plastic rocks** such as **rock salt, gypsum, ice, migmatite and gneiss**, which flow under pressure and heat, giving irregular, complex, convoluted (**ptygmatic**) folds.
5. **Fault-related folds.** Folds formed in association with the movement of thrust faults and related to them, such as **fault-bend folds** (where the thrust changes dip) and **fault-propagation folds** at the tip of the fault, and **drag folds** at the sides of a fault.
6. **Gravity (slump) folds.** Formed by **sliding and slumping of soft, unconsolidated sediments down a slope** under gravity, soon after deposition, which gives chaotic recumbent folds.

(A morphological classification, based on the form (anticline, syncline, symmetrical, asymmetrical, overturned, recumbent), is different from the genetic classification. A labelled block diagram of a buckle fold and a drape fold is credited.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Analyse the environmental effects of the eruptions of Mount Cameroon.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Mount Cameroon (Fako, 4 095 m)** is a large, active **basaltic strato-volcano** on the Cameroon Volcanic Line, near the coast of the Gulf of Guinea. Its eruptions are of **effusive to explosive (Strombolian)** type, with fluid basalt lava flows and cinder cones along fissures on the flanks, and it has erupted several times in the 20th and 21st centuries (for example 1982, 1999 and 2000, and 2012). The environmental effects are the following.

**Harmful effects.**
- **Lava flows** destroy the **forest and farm land**, such as the plantations (banana, oil palm, rubber) and food farms on the slopes, cover roads, and may threaten villages near the coast; where lava enters the sea, the coast is changed and marine life near the shore is killed.
- **Ash and cinders** fall on the leaves and cover the crops and the soil, which damages the plants, pollutes the water and causes breathing problems for people and animals.
- **Volcanic gases** (sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide) cause **air pollution and acid rain**, which damage vegetation and water, and carbon dioxide may collect in depressions and suffocate people and animals.
- **Fires, earthquakes (tremors), landslides and mudflows (lahars)** on the steep slopes in the heavy rains of the rainy season destroy habitats and block rivers; the **loss of the forest** on the slopes affects the plants and animals (the mountain is a centre of biodiversity with many endemic species).

**Beneficial effects.** The weathering of the basaltic ash and lava gives **very fertile volcanic soils**, which support dense farming populations and the large plantations around the mountain; the mountain is a source of **building materials (basalt, scoria)**, a **tourist attraction** (hiking), and its high relief produces very **heavy orographic rainfall** on the windward slopes.

**Conclusion:** the eruptions are of a moderate violence, but they cause local destruction of vegetation, farms and the environment, followed by the recovery of the vegetation on the new fertile soil.
